title: What Armstrong played in the early saloons
summary: Rose speculates about his repertoire: blues, popular pieces, Tiger Rag, Sister Kate, Bland songs.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: Oh, yeah. Uh, yeah. Uh, yeah. You know, what, when, when Louis started first working, like, in saloons, like, Matranga and, uh, in that area. Yeah. What, what, what was he playing? What, what, what do you think, what type of music was he playing? Well, he would have been playing the standard, he would have been playing a lot of blues.
Exactly. Yeah. Yeah.
That's what I would think of. Yeah, naturally.

And Louis always seemed to gravitate to the blues, anyway. Yeah. It was the kind of music that he really liked, and, and it, to a certain extent, put him out of step with the rest of the New Orleans musicians. Mm-hmm. Because they didn't play, uh, you know, blues as the main part of their action. Right. Um, but you have to consider what existed at that time musically.
Mm-hmm.
I know that, uh, he played in the Glowman, for instance. Mm-hmm. Which is by Ann Portescue Harrison. Mm-hmm. Of Bayou Road. And, uh, because it was an extremely popular piece around that time.
Mm-hmm.
And, uh, I'm sure he played Tiger Rag, or a version of Tiger Rag.
Yeah.
Uh, didn't have the title yet, but I'm sure he played it.
Yeah, yeah.
And, uh...
There were probably bits and pieces of a lot of melodies floating around.

And Sister Kate. Yeah. Would have been standard in his repertoire. Mm-hmm. Um, he probably also played songs of the Spanish-American War. Mm-hmm. Just before the Battle Mother. Mm-hmm. And, uh, I would be almost sure that he would have played that.
Uh-huh.

Um, I don't know, of course, what his repertoire was. Louie never said what his repertoire was. Of course he wouldn't remember. Mm-hmm. He wouldn't remember what he was playing in those days. Yeah. And most of the things that we think of that he should have been playing, weren't even written
yet.
Uh-huh. So you have to consider that. Yeah.
Well, that's what I'm about getting back to Snatch's melodies. Yeah. Probably floated around and were kind of a common base for... That's right.
For everybody.
For everybody. And then, years later, it was actually published and somebody took writer's credit for it. Yeah.

Certainly, uh, uh, James A. Bland's material had to be in his repertoire. Uh-huh. You know, like, uh... What songs? Oh Them Golden Slippers. Yeah. And, uh, In the Evening by the Moonlight. Mm-hmm. Those things had to be.
